learn.title: Real-Time Grid Supply Demand Balance
learn.intro: Electricity cannot be stored easily at scale, so the grid must match supply and demand every second. Understanding how grid operators balance fluctuating renewable sources with real-time consumption is essential for a reliable clean energy future.
learn.c1_text: Grid operators adjust power generation to keep frequency stable at 60 Hz in North America. If demand exceeds supply, frequency drops, triggering automatic generator responses. Think of it like adjusting water flow in a pipe system to maintain steady pressure.
learn.c2_text: AGC systems continuously monitor frequency and dispatch or reduce generation within seconds. Large power plants receive signals to ramp output up or down. This keeps the grid synchronized across regions, ensuring lights stay on even when clouds pass over solar farms.
learn.c3_text: India's National Load Generation Balance Authority (NLGCA) manages grid stability across states. With over 175 GW renewable capacity added by 2023, real-time scheduling and dispatch mechanisms ensure supply meets peak demand exceeding 200 GW during summer afternoons.

learn.stat2: Grid frequency maintained at 50 Hz ±3.5% in India
learn.stat3: USA: 70% of electricity from renewables during peak hours in April 2023

learn.title: Geothermal Energy Using Earth's Heat
learn.intro: Geothermal energy taps into Earth's internal heat for clean, baseload power and direct heating. Unlike solar and wind, geothermal provides consistent energy regardless of weather, making it a crucial complement to variable renewables.
learn.c1_text: Earth's core reaches temperatures of 6,000°C—hotter than the sun's surface. This heat drives plate tectonics and creates geothermal reservoirs. Accessing just 0.1% of this energy could power civilization for thousands of years, providing baseload power day and night.
learn.c2_text: Traditional geothermal requires natural hot water reservoirs. Enhanced Geothermal Systems inject water into hot dry rock to create artificial reservoirs. This technology could unlock geothermal potential across 90% of the U.S., dramatically expanding accessible resources beyond current sites.
learn.c3_text: India has identified 342 geothermal prospects across 8 states including Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, and Himachal Pradesh. The Himalayan region offers significant potential with estimated 10,000 MW exploitable capacity. Pilot projects in Tindharia demonstrate successful geothermal heating applications.

learn.title: Duck Curve Solar Grid Challenge
learn.intro: The duck curve illustrates how solar energy creates supply-demand mismatches when the sun sets. As solar generation drops rapidly in late afternoon, conventional power plants must quickly ramp up to meet evening electricity demand—a major challenge for grid operators.
learn.c1_text: The duck curve shows net load dipping during midday solar generation, then spiking sharply as solar fades after 5 PM. This shape resembles a duck, highlighting the need for rapid ramping capacity. California's grid operator CAISO first documented this phenomenon in 2013.
learn.c2_text: During the evening ramp, grid operators need power plants that can increase output by 13,000 MW within 3 hours. This requires flexible resources like natural gas turbines, hydroelectric plants, or battery storage systems capable of responding within minutes to maintain reliability.
learn.c3_text: India faces similar duck curve effects, particularly in Rajasthan and Gujarat with high solar penetration. Evening peak demand reaches 200+ GW while solar generation drops from 45 GW to near zero. The government promotes storage and flexible renewable integration to address this critical timing mismatch.

learn.title: Electric Commercial Vehicle Transition
learn.intro: Electrifying trucks and buses represents one of the most challenging yet impactful clean energy transitions. Heavy-duty vehicles account for 20% of transport emissions despite being only 10% of vehicles, making their electrification crucial for climate goals.
learn.c1_text: Battery-electric trucks work well for short-haul routes under 200 miles. Long-haul trucks may use hydrogen fuel cells for faster refueling and longer range. Buses typically use batteries since they follow predictable routes with overnight charging opportunities at depots.
learn.c2_text: Heavy-duty vehicles require specialized charging: 150 kW to 1 MW for trucks, 50-150 kW for buses. Depot charging works for fixed routes, while highway corridors need ultra-fast chargers. Grid upgrades and smart charging management are essential to handle concentrated power demands.
learn.c3_text: India's Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Hybrid & Electric Vehicles (FAME) scheme has deployed over 5,000 electric buses across 70 cities. Delhi alone operates 2,000+ electric buses. The government plans 500,000 electric buses by 2030 to reduce urban air pollution and transport emissions.

learn.title: EV Charging Levels Explained
learn.intro: Understanding EV charging options helps consumers choose the right setup for their needs. From overnight home charging to highway fast-charging networks, different levels serve different use cases in the growing electric vehicle ecosystem.
learn.c1_text: Level 1 uses standard 120V household outlets, adding 2-5 miles of range per hour of charging. Perfect for overnight top-ups and low daily driving needs. While slow, it requires no installation costs and works anywhere with a standard electrical outlet, ideal for apartment dwellers.
learn.c2_text: Level 2 uses 240V outlets, adding 10-60 miles per hour—enough for full overnight charging. DC fast chargers deliver 100-200+ miles in 15-30 minutes but cost $50,000-$100,000 and require commercial electrical infrastructure. Best for long trips and fleet operations.
learn.c3_text: India plans 330,000 public charging stations by 2030. The Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Hybrid & Electric Vehicles (FAME) scheme supports both AC Level 2 and DC fast chargers. Delhi has over 1,000 public charging points, with major highways getting fast-charging corridors.

learn.title: Green Hydrogen Production Technologies
learn.intro: Green hydrogen produced via water electrolysis using renewable electricity offers a clean fuel for hard-to-electrify sectors like steelmaking and shipping. Different electrolyzer technologies—PEM and alkaline—each offer distinct advantages for various applications.
learn.c1_text: Electrolysis splits water into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity. Green hydrogen requires renewable-powered electrolyzers to achieve zero emissions. Current efficiency reaches 70-80%, with costs dropping from $16/kg in 2020 to $4-6/kg for new projects in favorable locations.
learn.c3_text: India launched a $2.3 billion National Green Hydrogen Mission targeting 5 MMT annual production by 2030. The initiative focuses on manufacturing electrolyzers domestically and creating demand in steel, fertilizer, and refining sectors. Pilot projects in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu demonstrate commercial viability.
